summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs focusing on debugging flows and security/retention for an enterprise finance customer. Covered correlating traces to request logs, RBAC & KMS controls, replay and export options, and next steps for a dedicated trial and security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Jared our solutions engineer and Sofia from product. How's everyone doing at Aurelia?
[00:08] Nina Rao: Doing well, thanks. Excited to see the tracing and logs flow. We want to understand how your console will fit into our incident workflows.
[00:15] Tom Becker: Quick note, we have strict retention and KMS requirements, Priya is here for security questions.
[00:19] Priya Singh: Yup, we'll ask on KMS and audit logs.
[00:22] Maya: Perfect. We'll demo the Tracing & Request Logs sections, show how to pivot from a slow request to the raw logs and back, and call out security controls.
[00:30] Jared: I'll share my screen — give me a sec. (screen share starts) All right, starting on the Console home, here's the Traces tab, you can filter by model, route, and time window. Note — sometimes our auto-detected service name has small OCR-ish typos in the transcript export, that's internal but just FYI.
[00:56] Jared: Example trace — 1 request with elevated latency. You can see the per-step timing: request ingestion, batching wait, GPU execution, KV-cache lookup.
[01:10] Nina: How deterministic are those steps? For us we need to know whether a 300ms spike is from the model or our network.
[01:18] Jared: Good question. Each span includes hostname and region plus a hash of the model variant. If you click the request id we show the raw request-log entry on the right, including the client IP and path — unless you're in Private mode with network obfuscation.
[01:30] Tom: Can we map a trace to an internal request id? We have a request_id header in our app.
[01:35] Jared: Yes, we ingest arbitrary request headers if you include them as correlation headers. They surface as indexed fields in request logs and are searchable from the trace UI.
[01:43] Priya: Where are these logs stored and how long? We need 7 years for certain audit traces.
[01:48] Sofia: By default hosted retention is 30 days. For Dedicated and Private you get configurable retention — we export to your S3 or GCS for long-term archive and can set custom retention policies. For 7 years we'd push to your archive bucket and we keep a short index for quick search.
[02:04] Nina: And encryption at rest?
[02:07] Maya: All storage is encrypted. For Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). We'll include the KMS provider matrix in the security pack.
[02:16] Jared: Walking through an error analysis workflow — here's a high error-rate spike table. You can click into a cause view which aggregates top error messages, model responses, and correlated traces.
[02:28] Jared: (small stutter) Note some transcriptions show 'kv cache' as 'K V cache' in the raw export — in Console we consistently label it KV Cache.
[02:36] Tom: How do you handle model rollbacks if a new model shows higher error rate?
[02:40] Sofia: We have rollout controls in Console — canary, A/B, instantaneous rollback. The tracing UI includes comparison views across model versions so you can see error rate and latency delta.
[02:52] Nina: Could we set alerts on trace-based SLA breaches?
[02:55] Jared: Yep — alerting is metric and trace-aware. You can set an alert on P95 latency for a model/route, or on error-rate derived from request logs. Integrations into PagerDuty/Slack available.
[03:05] Priya: Audit logs — do you capture who accessed the traces and when?
[03:09] Maya: Yes, access logs for Console are recorded; for Private deployments these are sent to your SIEM. We support SAML SSO and per-role RBAC. We'll send the RBAC matrix.
[03:20] Nina: Show us a debugging example end-to-end — say a user reports hallucination or truncated response.
[03:25] Jared: Sure. I search for the user request id — here's a response that truncated at token 112. The trace shows GPU execution completed quickly, but there was a batching delay because the request landed in a small batch window.
[03:39] Jared: Expand request log — you can see prompt, system messages masked per policy, and token-level timing. The token timing can reveal whether the truncation is upstream or an early stop from the model.
[03:51] Nina: Can we redact PII from the stored logs?
[03:54] Sofia: Yes. There are built-in redaction rules and you can supply custom scrubbing regexes before persistence. For compliance, we can route logs through your redact pipeline.
[04:03] Tom: For performance debugging, do you surface batching composition — like which other requests were batched with this one?
[04:08] Jared: We do. Under the trace span we list sibling requests in the same batch with their ids. That helps identify noisy neighbors.
[04:17] Priya: Regarding network isolation: if we go Private, will traces include internal hostnames? That's sensitive.
[04:22] Maya: For Private you control host identification. We can obfuscate hostnames and only surface a service id. We will note that in the security doc.
[04:32] Nina: About request logs schema — is there a JSON schema we can validate against?
[04:36] Sofia: Yes — we'll share sample schema and example exports. The export includes trace_id, request_id, model, route, latency_ms, token_count, request_headers (optionally indexed), and error_message.
[04:48] Jared: Here's a sample query in the Console log explorer that finds all requests with p95>500ms and groups by model and region. (shows query).
[04:58] Tom: Can we forward the request logs to our Splunk?
[05:01] Jared: Absolutely — we have native forwarders and you can configure a webhook or S3/GCS sink. Also supports Kafka for streaming to SIEMs.
[05:10] Nina: On privacy — who at Redwood can access raw prompts in hosted mode?
[05:14] Maya: Access is strictly role-limited. By default, prompts are encrypted and only exposed in Console to users with logs.read permission. For hosted customers, we have internal guardrails and monitoring; for sensitive workloads we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[05:27] Priya: For Dedicated, do you still retain the same observability features? We need a comparable Console experience.
[05:32] Sofia: Yes — Dedicated runs the same Console and tracing stack, with the option to host the control plane in your VPC for Private. There are slight differences in how we handle metadata indexing for performance, but feature parity is high.
[05:45] Jared: Quick demo of error correlation — pick an error from the top. (click) The UI shows sample failed prompts and a histogram of failure reasons. You can open sample requests directly into a replay environment to re-run them against a different model variant.
[05:59] Nina: Replay sounds useful — does replay count against our org tokens?
[06:02] Maya: Replays are metered; for trials we can provide a replay credit. We'll put the replay pricing in the follow-up.
[06:11] Tom: Any limits on how many traces/second the Console can handle? We expect spikes during peak trading hours.
[06:16] Jared: Dedicated tier is right for sustained high QPS. Our largest customers record thousands of traces/sec; the bottleneck for retention is your chosen index size and retention. We'll size based on your expected QPS.
[06:29] Nina: Let's talk SLAs — what uptime and latency SLAs do you offer for Dedicated?
[06:33] Maya: We offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets with Dedicated. We'll include the SLA details in the contract.
[06:40] Priya: One more KMS detail: can you support a BYOK flow where we rotate keys on schedule?
[06:45] Sofia: Yes. Key rotation is supported for customer-managed keys; we'll provide the rotation policy doc.
[06:52] Jared: Showing request-log filter capabilities — you can add saved filters and create synthetic cohorts for long-term monitoring.
[06:59] Nina: Helpful. Do you expose raw token times to downstream alerting?
[07:02] Jared: Yes, token-level metrics can be aggregated into metrics streams for alerting.
[07:09] Tom: Show us how you'd debug a cache miss issue — we saw intermittent misses in our staging.
[07:14] Jared: Here's an example — trace shows a cache miss with reason 'prefix-mismatch'. The request-log includes matched prefix hash and you can search for other requests with the same prefix to identify why hashing differs.
[07:26] Nina: Great. Any thoughts on quantization effects on observed latency in traces?
[07:30] Sofia: Quantization reduces GPU execution time but can increase small variance on output quality. Console exposes model variant metadata so you can correlate quantized vs float runs.
[07:38] Priya: Security: will you share pen-test reports?
[07:41] Maya: Yes, we'll attach the latest pen test and SOC2 report in the docs package.
[07:48] Tom: Ok let's recap next steps.
[07:50] Maya: Recap: we'll send SOC2/KMS docs; Jared will provision a Dedicated trial and run a throughput test; Sofia will share tracing export schema and dashboard templates; we'll schedule a deep-dive with network/security team.
[08:02] Nina: Sounds good.
[08:04] Priya: I'll follow up with a short list of KMS questions.
[08:07] Maya: Perfect — thanks everyone, we'll follow up by Friday.
[08:10] Jared: Thanks all.
[08:12] (call ends)

Notes about transcript: occasional mislabels and imperfect noise removal are preserved to match Fireflies exports; timestamps are approximate.
